entries.title: Patient portals get real names — and syncs tell you whose data arrived
entries.body: If your health system's portal was swallowed by a merger (MyChart, we see you), Allos now keeps a registry of portals under Settings → Integrations, with each connected account mapped to the profile it feeds. Sync reports name the portal and the person, so a household with two MyChart logins can finally tell whose labs just landed. Identities Allos hasn't seen before are surfaced instead of guessed at — nothing is ever silently filed to the wrong person.

entries.title: Upload documents from anywhere — tokens, an API, and a tiny CLI
entries.body: You can now mint API tokens under Settings → Account & security: login-tied, scoped to document upload only, shown once, and revocable per device. With one, a new authenticated endpoint accepts document uploads from outside the browser — same ingest pipeline, same per-profile dedup, honest per-file results — and a dependency-free command-line script uploads a folder of files from any machine. Name a token per device so retiring one never disturbs the others.

entries.title: Nudges that read like they know you
entries.body: A sweep over every message the app sends. The protein line now says when you've reached your goal instead of implying a shortfall; the workout nudge leads with the exact target driving its suggestion; the daily digest previews today's recommended workout and drops its redundant tail on Telegram. A second same-day workout nudge acknowledges the session you already did, and if mood check-ins are about to auto-pause, the final reminder says so — pausing quietly unless you ask to keep them.

entries.title: The safety tier stops lying
entries.body: Missed-dose escalations now reach every channel you configured — Web Push and Home Assistant included, not just Telegram — and a broken safety channel finally shows up in delivery health. Escalations state how long a dose has been unconfirmed and offer a one-tap Skip. The /dose command shows the same redose safety verdicts as the app, push notifications stop asking you to tap buttons they can't show, a next-morning tap on yesterday's household round is refused instead of mislogged, and shared-chat messages always name whose dose they mean.

entries.title: Imaging saves show up reliably — and failures say so
entries.body: Adding an imaging study could occasionally leave the list unchanged even though the save landed, because the page's refresh path pointed at a redirect stub. Saves now repaint the imaging list directly, and a refused submission shows its error instead of silently rendering nothing.

entries.title: Biomarkers on your phone: results first
entries.body: On a phone, the Biomarkers page used to open with nearly 1,900 pixels of summary cards before the first actual panel of results. The panel index now leads — visible on the first screen — with the trajectory warning keeping its headline up top and folding its details, while the starred lens and bio-age cards follow whole below. Desktop is unchanged.

entries.title: Broken syncs finally speak up — and food taps count right
entries.body: A revoked or persistently failing integration used to sit quietly on-device while your data went stale. The morning digest now names each broken source with a link to fix it, and a connection that simply stopped syncing — recording nothing at all — raises its own attention item with per-provider staleness thresholds. Also fixed: tapping a Telegram food nudge outside its original window now counts toward the right meal, so the button's (n) tally matches what you actually logged.

entries.title: Journal search now searches your whole history
entries.body: Searching or filtering the training log used to look only at the days already loaded on screen — a matching workout from months ago simply didn't exist as far as the page knew. Search and every filter now query your entire ledger, paging over the matches themselves, with a new source filter and a fault count that reflects your whole history. An unfiltered journal loads exactly as fast as before.

entries.title: Cycle tracking stops lying to you — in both directions
entries.body: The "Period started today" quick action no longer confirms success when nothing was written — it tells you a period is already open, refuses an implausibly soon restart, and shows where you are in your cycle instead of offering the wrong button the moment a period ends. A one-tap "Still bleeding" reopens a just-ended period. And a forgotten "ended" tap no longer reads as menstrual forever: after ten days the app treats the period as probably over and asks you to set the end date — your record is never changed behind your back. New entries are checked for overlaps, future dates, and impossible ranges, with every refusal naming the conflict.

entries.title: Your half-entered workout survives anything
entries.body: Long forms now keep a local draft as you type: reload, crash, or a deploy mid-entry, and a banner offers your unsaved work back — Resume or Discard, your choice, never applied silently, always cleared once you actually save. Drafts stay on your device only and are wiped on logout. App updates also stopped yanking pages out from under you: a new version now waits with a small "Update ready" note, and you reload when you're ready — it even mentions if you have unsaved work open.

entries.title: A tidier supplement shelf and medicine cabinet
entries.body: The supplements page puts your working list back ahead of the safety reading, with a "More supplements" disclosure matching Food's. The medicine cabinet got a matching pass: profile-aware links back to each item, actions tucked into a standard overflow menu, and the usual delete confirmation. Linking a shared supply now confirms it worked and no longer lets a double-tap create duplicate bottles, and same-named linked items disambiguate by kind and dose so you always know which one you're looking at.

entries.title: Upcoming stops drowning you in routine
entries.body: The planning page's scheduled doses now fold into one line per band — "14 doses today · 9 taken" — expandable to the exact rows with their confirm buttons intact, and routine interaction/gene notes roll up the same way. Safety never folds: a missed-dose escalation or an as-needed limit warning always renders individually, above the fold, and allergy conflicts keep their place at the top. The genuinely attention-worthy items stop being needles in a haystack.

entries.title: File a document or log a practice without leaving where you are
entries.body: The quick-log sheet gains an Add document row that opens the familiar upload form in place — camera included, so photographing a paper result is one tap — and a Log practice row listing your tracked practices with this week's standing. The command palette learned both too: search for "scan" or "lab report" to file a document, or type "log sauna" to record a practice — a bare practice name stays a search, so you never log by accident.

entries.title: Weekly, alternating-day, and taper schedules — without giving up reminders
entries.body: Intake items can finally say when they actually happen: weekly (methotrexate, a GLP-1 shot), alternating days, every N days, or specific weekdays. A weekly medication now reminds and escalates on its day and stays silent the other six — no more choosing between daily nagging and demoting it to no reminders at all. Off-day quick-logs still work and ask an honest confirm; adherence math counts only the days a dose was actually owed.

entries.title: Charts you can actually read on a phone — and a day chart you can touch
entries.body: Chart text now has a real minimum: labels are sized against how small the chart can actually render, so nothing shrinks below legibility (two charts were quietly under the floor and got fixed). The day-at-a-glance chart labels your wake and bed times, names its activity blocks, and drops the machine-analysis tick marks. The intraday chart gained a touch layer: scrub for an exact heart-rate reading, drag or tap to zoom, all with the keyboard supported — and annotation labels now stay inside the plot instead of smearing past its edge.

entries.title: Search finally knows your whole record
entries.body: Global search and record Q&A now cover nine domains that were previously unsearchable: providers, imaging, genomics, dental, skin lesions, illness episodes, protocols, wellness practices, and equipment. Hits deep-link straight to the right detail page, providers only surface through your own records that name them, and asking a question can now cite any of these domains as evidence.

entries.title: Skin lesions and allergies join the visit trail
entries.body: The last two clinical observations without a visit link now have one: a skin lesion or an allergy can be tied to the encounter where it was noted, and an allergy can also record which provider confirmed it. They join the same link, suggestion, and unlink flow every other record type uses, and imported allergy records pick up their visit automatically when the document names one. Deleting a visit never deletes the observation — the record outlives the appointment.

entries.title: Trends opens on one page: your stars, then your body
entries.body: The Overview and Body tabs merged into a single landing surface: the trending digest up top, your starred cards in the order you arranged them, and the full body census streaming in below — now one flat ranked stack instead of titled boxes, so your stars and the everyday-first order decide what leads. Fitness, Nutrition, and Insights remain their own tabs. Old bookmarks to the Body tab land on the merged page, and the page arrives as fast as the old Overview tab did alone.

entries.title: The review inbox now tells you what to double-check
entries.body: Document extraction now reports how sure it was about each captured row. The import detail page gains a "Check these first" card that ranks the least-certain rows to the top with the model's stated reason, and Data → Review badges each document with how many rows deserve a look. Nothing is blocked or hidden by this — a document extracted before this feature simply shows no badge, and a row the model was confident about behaves exactly as before.

entries.title: Must, should, may: your supplements and meds now carry an honest obligation
entries.body: Priority levels and the separate as-needed flag collapse into one clear setting: must (missing it is an incident — reminders and escalation), should (reminded and counted, never escalated), and may (never pushed, no misses — it simply stays one tap away in its usual slot). Rarely-taken supplements get a gentle Demote offer on their own reminder, never a new notification; accepting moves them into a calm "available" shelf on Upcoming instead of deleting anything. Medications default to must, and lowering one spells out exactly what safety net you are giving up — while interaction, gene, and upper-limit warnings fire identically no matter the level. Daily digests now lead with what actually changed — notably missed and resumed — instead of a fraction.

entries.title: Wellness practices grow up: findable, editable, and safely deletable
entries.body: The Wellness page now shows up in navigation, recent pages, and the command palette. Practices gained the full lifecycle they were missing: cadence rules that refuse impossible values out loud, protection against two practices silently sharing one history, session editing, a shared history/progress/heatmap view, and — at last — the choice between stop tracking (keeps your history) and permanent deletion (with undo). Protocol pages were tightened alongside, and protocol outcomes now rank by which biomarkers actually have before-and-after data to show.

entries.title: All your scans, one source — and a strict mode that means it
entries.body: Readings extracted from medical documents used to be one source per report, so "my DEXA scans" could never be picked as a single series. The source picker now offers Documents — every report together — and the comparison chart draws them as one sparse line alongside the per-report series. Pair it with the new "Only this source" checkbox and the chart shows exactly that source: days it did not cover stay honestly empty instead of borrowing another source's number, totals count only its rows, and latest-value tiles show an empty state rather than a stand-in. Unchecking restores the familiar fallback behavior exactly.

entries.title: Routes settle into their real homes
entries.body: A housekeeping sweep with a few visible edges: the Healthspan page is now consistently called Longevity everywhere it appears, and a long tail of retired internal redirects is gone now that every link in the app points straight at the real page. If you bookmarked one of the very old addresses, update the bookmark to the page you land on from the navigation. Under the hood, dead route scaffolding was removed and shared reads moved next to the pages that use them, which keeps future changes safer.

entries.title: Pin your Body cards with a star — and the default order finally makes sense
entries.body: The Trends Body tab now honors a ★ on any card: starred cards jump to the top and stay there, and you can drag your starred set into whatever sequence you like from Overview. Unstar a card and it returns to its ranked slot. The ranked default underneath was re-sequenced to lead with everyday metrics (weight, sleep, steps) instead of burying them, and life-stage cards (like cycle tracking) keep their place above everything when they apply.

entries.title: The 'just recovered' dashboard calms down — and dismissals finally stick
entries.body: After an illness ends, the dashboard used to stack three separate household bands. They now fold into one coherent recovered state: the reopen line carries the household-history link inline, the household strip absorbs it during the 8–14-day tail, and a quiet household shows the link without conjuring an empty strip. Dismissing the "Recently resolved — reopen?" line now sticks across reloads — it was the only X in the app that came back — while other caregivers on their own logins still see it, and nothing about the reopen window itself changes. The Now strip also stacks its two cards full-width on phones instead of squeezing them side by side.

entries.title: Registries live where you use them, and an empty Timeline points somewhere
entries.body: The medicine cabinet left the sidebar: like the equipment registry, it's now reached from where you actually use it — doors on the Medications page, the Supplements tab, and Household — and visiting either registry highlights its parent nav section instead of stranding you with nothing lit. Every old URL still works. A brand-new profile's empty Timeline now offers real next steps (log something, connect a source, upload a document) instead of a bare "No timeline events yet." — and only when the account is genuinely empty, never when a filter simply matched nothing.

entries.title: Invites without passwords, and honest answers at the door
entries.body: Inviting someone to your instance got simpler and safer. With an email invite, you no longer invent an interim password for them — the account is unusable until they set their own through the invite link. New logins can be granted profile access at creation (defaulting sensibly when a same-named profile exists), so nobody lands in an account that can see nothing. And if a login does end up without access — say its last grant was revoked — signing in now says so plainly instead of silently bouncing back to the form, stale sessions are cleaned up rather than lingering as "active", and the attempt is recorded for the admin. Profiles with identical names are now told apart everywhere you pick one. Also: asking your records a plural question ("any allergies?") now finds singular-named entries.

entries.title: Every icon button explains itself
entries.body: All 96 icon-only buttons in the app — including every Delete and Remove — now show a tooltip on hover and carry a proper screen-reader name. A build-time guard keeps it that way: a new icon button can't ship without one. On touch screens, where there is no hover, every destructive icon action already asks for confirmation before acting — that safety net is now enforced too.

entries.title: Your protein goal is finally yours to set
entries.body: The protein band on the Nutrition gauge has always adapted to a training goal — but there was nowhere to set one, so everyone silently sat on the "Active" band. Settings → Nutrition now has the picker (RDA baseline / Active / Muscle gain / Cut), saving as you change it, with the band shown in real g/kg terms. It's an informational range, not a prescription. Two consistency fixes rode along: each dashboard insight now appears in exactly one card (data-quality gaps no longer show in both the Data quality widget and the Coaching observations rollup — and hiding the widget hands its items back to the rollup instead of losing them), and "activity streak" now means one thing everywhere — the rest-tolerant streak; the strict consecutive-days number, where it appears, is labeled as exactly that.

entries.title: Screening scores can be corrected, and the passport learns what forms ask
entries.body: A mistyped PHQ-9 or AUDIT-C score is no longer permanent: screening results now offer Correct and Remove, with removal undoable — and correcting a score below threshold releases the crisis banner it tripped. Allergies gain the fields that make them real safety data: criticality (could a future exposure be life-threatening?), verification status (suspected / confirmed / refuted), and multiple graded reactions per allergen — a refuted allergy stops gating your medication checks, and high-criticality allergies lead the emergency card. Immunizations gain lot number, route, and site — what school, travel, and employment forms actually ask — plus structured exemption types for declinations. Everything unstated stays unstated; existing records keep meaning exactly what they meant.

entries.title: The Biomarkers index shows itself whole — and fits a phone
entries.body: The Biomarkers browser dropped its pager: the collapsed panel index is its own natural bound, so panels never straddle a page break, counts are always whole, and opening a group survives every filter change. Sorting defaults to name (newest reading first under each), the panel filter only offers panels that can actually return results for the surfaces the browser shows, and on phones the starred card and the biological-age hero fold behind honest toggles — reclaiming about 740 vertical pixels so the index is far closer to the first screen.

entries.title: Machine-aware progress reaches comparisons, Trends, PRs, and goals
entries.body: The equipment-aware strength tracking from earlier today now runs end to end. The Trends strength-progression chart shows one labeled series per machine ("Machine Chest Press (Hotel chest press)") instead of blending them; personal records are per-machine everywhere they appear — Trends, Training, the weekly recap, and coaching; the Analyze comparison offers a labeled machine picker so you compare like against like; and a weight goal can now name the machine it's set on. Goals you already have keep their movement-wide meaning — nothing re-scopes — and a goal that names no machine still counts every context. Deleting equipment widens its goals back to movement-wide rather than orphaning them.

entries.title: Corrected lab results stop erasing history — and readings learn how they were drawn
entries.body: When a lab re-issues a result — a corrected potassium, an amended differential — the previous value is now preserved beside the reading instead of being silently overwritten: the biomarker page shows "Corrected — was 5.2 mmol/L" under the live value, which never charts or counts twice. Readings can also record their result status (preliminary / final / corrected / amended), whether the draw was fasting, the specimen (serum, plasma, urine…), and the clinician who ordered the test separately from the lab that ran it. Everything stays honest by default: an unstated attribute stays unstated — never a guessed "final" or "non-fasting" — and your own hand-corrected readings are still never touched by a re-sync. One filing fix rode along: a freeform lab spelling now files under its family's clinical panel instead of stranding in "Other".

entries.title: Syncs stop overstating themselves
entries.body: Three honesty fixes for Data → Review. A Strava, Oura, or Withings sync cut short by the provider (a page cap or rate limit) now shows a caution icon and a "partial" chip with a plain explanation — the next sync picks up where it left off — instead of reading as a clean green run. A phone push that fails partway now reports exactly which records landed before the stop, with the same drill-in as a successful sync. And Weather & UV finally has a home in Review's Connected sources, so its sync history is reachable from its settings page. Separately, two devices that agree on a reading — say both recorded 55 bpm resting heart rate — no longer appear in Review as a conflict to resolve: identical numbers are normal multi-source coverage, and only genuine disagreements ask for your decision. Recovery baselines now count each day once, however many devices covered it.

entries.title: Your strength history knows which machine you were on
entries.body: Two chest-press machines — home and hotel — used to share one progression: the app would seed the hotel machine with the home machine's 80 kg and blend both into one PR track and one plateau signal. Sets have always recorded which registered equipment they were performed on; now the history, suggestions, comparisons, and plateau detection respect it. A freshly registered machine starts clean instead of borrowing another machine's numbers, plateau alerts name the machine they're about, and dismissing one machine's alert leaves the other's live. You can also register new equipment right inside the workout form — logging on an unfamiliar gym's machine no longer means abandoning your in-progress session. One heads-up: previously dismissed plateau notices may reappear once as their tracking keys migrate; dismiss them again and they stay dismissed.

entries.title: A1c reminders keep their quarterly clock
entries.body: Labs often report Hemoglobin A1c alongside its estimated-average-glucose re-expression from one draw. When the eAG line happened to be the newest reading, the retest reminder silently fell back to a generic annual interval instead of the quarterly cadence A1c calls for — exactly wrong for the people tracking it most closely. Every member of a biomarker family now shares the family's retest clock and its reminder reads consistently ("Retest Hemoglobin A1c"), and a freeform lab spelling the catalog doesn't list can no longer show up twice for the same draw or be counted as two different current readings.

entries.title: The strength editor works like a phone app on phones
entries.body: Logging sets at the gym got a real phone layout. Each set is now two clean rows — "Set 3" with its RPE, warm-up, and remove controls on one line, full-width weight × reps steppers underneath — instead of three disconnected bands. The exercise header gives the lift name the whole row, so "Barbell Bench Press" no longer truncates, and the how-to, reorder, and remove buttons moved to their own toolbar with proper finger-sized targets. Desktop keeps its familiar compact table.

entries.title: Fitbit archive imports: right categories, honest accounting
entries.body: Exercises imported from a Fitbit (Google Takeout) archive now land as what they actually were: stationary bike, jump rope, rowing machine, Tabata, TRX, rollerblading and dozens more get the correct activity category and grouping, and meditation sessions become wellness practices instead of workouts. Your existing history is corrected automatically — rows you hand-edited are left untouched. The importer also reports honestly in Data → Review: every attempt appears with what it inserted, updated, or skipped, you can drill into exactly which records a run wrote, and an import that fails partway now says precisely what landed before it stopped — and is always safe to re-run.

entries.title: Protocols round out: one-tap logging, read-only endings, day-by-day heatmaps
entries.body: Logging an intervention now takes one tap from the protocol itself — activity, food-group, and wellness-practice interventions each hand off to their own logging form, from the detail page or the dashboard widget. Ended protocols become read-only for new experiment data (you can still fix a mis-logged session or run it again), so a finished experiment's numbers stay what they were. And every protocol card gains a per-day heatmap of its window — see at a glance which days you actually did the thing, with a compact rendering for long windows and phones.

entries.title: Protocol lifecycle grows up: modal editing, resume, run again
entries.body: Edit, End, Delete, Resume, and Run again now live together in the protocol page's ⋯ menu. A protocol ended in the last 7 days can resume in place as if nothing happened; an older one starts a fresh run while keeping the historical record intact. Creating and editing both open in the same roomy modal instead of the narrow list rail, and destructive confirmations use the app's own dialogs — no more native browser popups.

entries.title: The docs caught up with the app
entries.body: The README is now a real product and self-hosting guide, and the feature reference describes the app as it actually is today — retired navigation, old settings layouts, and already-shipped work are no longer described as current or future behavior. If you set up Allos from the docs, they now tell the truth end to end.

entries.title: Starting a protocol got much lighter
entries.body: The New protocol form no longer sits fully expanded on the Longevity page — it opens in place when you ask for it, with protocol templates built into the same form (template deep links still work). Picking what to measure is a searchable selector with sensible ranking, familiar aliases, and selected chips, instead of a wall of hundreds of checkboxes. Measures that exist as both a body metric and a lab value are now one logical choice, with same-day readings preferring your scale's number.

entries.title: Your lab history, folded into panels you can scan
entries.body: The Biomarkers list — the longest page in the app — now groups your readings by clinical panel: each panel shows as one line with its analyte count and how many are currently flagged ("Lipids · 6 · 1 flagged"), and taps open to the readings. Flagged panels identify themselves at a glance, searching or filtering opens the matching groups automatically, and the roughly ten separate trajectory-watch cards folded into a single expandable card (each item can still be dismissed individually). Entry forms sit behind "+ Add". The page dropped from about thirteen thousand pixels to under three thousand.

entries.title: Wellness practices become first-class
entries.body: Sauna, meditation, red light, breathwork — practices now have their own home on the Wellness surface: define a practice, set a weekly cadence target, log sessions with time and duration, and correct history when you got it wrong. Practices show up properly in protocols, Upcoming, and the dashboard, and route to their own logging flow instead of the training editor. Renaming a practice keeps its whole history and targets attached, regardless of capitalization or spacing.

entries.title: Search results take you to the thing you searched for
entries.body: Picking an activity from the command palette now opens that day's Timeline instead of the generic Training page (which, if you were already on it, made the palette look broken — nothing changed on screen). A medication result opens that medication's page, a vaccine result opens its per-vaccine page with your dose history and schedule, and a goal lands on the goals tab. Biomarker names also got a cleanup: rows now show the clean catalog name ("Uric Acid") instead of the lab's shouting case ("URIC ACID") wherever the reading is the point — import-review and "as reported" views deliberately keep the document's original text.

entries.title: Trends ties off: annotation controls in the context bar, complete saved views, honest volume bars
entries.body: The event/protocol-window toggles moved into the context bar's expanded controls — one set for the whole page instead of a repeated row above each chart, returning about 60px on phones. A saved view now captures everything about where you were, including the Body tab's tiles-vs-all layout, and views saved under the old tab names keep working. The range pills scroll with a fade when they overflow a phone screen, training volume draws as bars instead of a noisy line, and the normalize toggle is finally finger-sized.

entries.title: Your labs, organized by panel — everywhere
entries.body: Allos now knows which clinical panel every catalog biomarker belongs to — Lipids, Complete blood count, Thyroid, and thirty-one more. The Timeline titles a lab draw by what was measured ("Lipids results — 6 results, 1 out of range") instead of the lab company's name; the Biomarkers list can filter by panel as a real clinical facet; and each biomarker's detail page offers the rest of its panel one tap away. Readings the catalog doesn't recognize keep their original grouping.

entries.title: Trends charts open in the order that matters for you
entries.body: The Body tab's default chart order now starts from who the profile is: growth charts lead for a child, the series your active conditions watch (blood pressure for hypertension, oxygen for asthma) move up, a metric with a live goal rises, and empty charts can never sit above charts with data. Nothing reshuffles day to day — the order comes from stable facts, not the latest sync — and once you drag your own arrangement, it's yours permanently.

entries.title: Nutrition gets one workspace for food and supplements
entries.body: The Nutrition page was redesigned around a shared Food | Supplements workspace: the same recent-day and time-slot controls on both tabs, compact date menus on phones, supplement add/edit in a focused modal, and date-specific protein and fiber feedback with weekly summaries. Meals you log for an earlier day now stay on that day's slot. Supplement schedules also stopped showing newly added doses on days before the dose existed — history stays honest.

entries.title: Phone screens: metric details, the view strip, and Timeline all slim down
entries.body: Three phone-size cleanups. A metric's detail page no longer shows three identical stat cards when you have under a week of data — coincident windows collapse into one honestly-labelled card, the “Change” stat names the actual date it compares against, a caption notes when your selected range outruns the data, and step/hydration/calorie charts now start their axis at zero. The view strip at the top of list pages drops its card frame on phones, returning about 30px of every screen to content. And the Timeline: the day switcher stays pinned while you scroll, the filter block collapses to a single summary line, and symptom entry sits behind “+ Log symptom” — opening automatically on days that already have symptoms or an active illness.

entries.title: Tap any chart to go deeper — and edit its readings
entries.body: Every full-size chart on Trends now links through to a detail view — tap the title or the expand icon; the plot itself still pans and zooms without hijacking your touch. Charts that summarize several things (nutrition macros, training volume, heart-rate zones) land on their real home pages, and the sun/outdoor-time chart — the tab's last dead end — gets a detail page of its own. Each metric detail page also gains a Readings table: every stored reading, with in-place edit and delete. A reading you hand-correct is protected from being overwritten by the next sync, and a deleted one stays deleted.

entries.title: Health Connect syncs catch more duplicates — and more readings
entries.body: Fixes from real-world payloads: possible-duplicate detection now groups same-day readings even when the source apps label their type differently, so cross-app duplicates actually surface for review; skin-temperature variation — the one reading that can legitimately be negative — is now accepted instead of dropped; and sleep-stage durations keep their precision instead of rounding.

entries.title: Trends chrome gets out of the way — and tiles drag
entries.body: On a phone, Trends now opens with a one-line context bar — "Overview · 90D" — instead of two rows of pills and tabs: tap it to change the range or tab, and it slides away with the top bar as you scroll, returning the moment you scroll up. The window label is always visible, so a chart is never shown without knowing what period you're looking at. Your first chart now sits inside the opening screen. Reordering saved tiles is a long-press drag — the same gesture the dashboard uses — with the up/down controls still available in each tile's menu. This also fixed a bug where those arrows sometimes visibly did nothing.

entries.title: Training opens on what you're doing today
entries.body: The Training overview now leads with today's session, then your week, with everything else in calm order behind it — and the wall of per-muscle coaching notices is one expandable card (each notice can still be dismissed individually inside it). The long PR lists show their top three with the rest one tap away, and the charts moved to Trends → Fitness where the date range applies to them. The page is about half its former height, and switching tabs no longer does the work of building all six behind the scenes.

entries.title: Trends → Fitness respects your date range
entries.body: The Fitness tab stopped mirroring the Training page and became true trends content: four sections — volume (as bars, with the activity heatmap sized to your window), zones and cardio, strength progression, and sport — all honoring the same date range as every other tab. Records set in your window show as a top-three list with the full history one tap away on Training. Old links into the tab's former sub-tabs land correctly.

entries.title: A logged workout is a logged workout — and day one reads honestly
entries.body: Two fixes to how the app reads your data. Logging a finished session with just a duration ("Walking, 30 minutes, done") no longer convinces every page you're mid-workout — the live dock, the "Still working out?" nag, and the household chip now correctly treat it as completed. And a medication added moments ago no longer shows "0% adherence" — the worst possible number for "no history yet": days before a dose existed don't count against it, the card simply shows no percentage until there's real history, and a week where you genuinely missed every dose keeps its honest 0%. Medications brought in from an imported record keep their full history.

entries.title: The update notice stops floating, and small fixes land where you log
entries.body: The "Refresh to update" notice after a server update is now a banner at the top of the page instead of a permanent floating bubble over the bottom corner of your phone — same message, out of your way. Toasts and the offline pill also learned to stack above the live-workout dock instead of covering it. In the activity editor, the Form check section now appears while you're still creating an activity (as soon as it autosaves), the reps steppers finally step down as well as up, and the phone bar drops its repeat-last button — that shortcut lives in search and each journal card's menu, where it always also lived.

entries.title: Five Trends tabs, and Compare finds its home
entries.body: The Trends strip is down to five tabs in the order you actually use them — Overview, Body, Fitness, Nutrition, Insights — and all five now fit a phone screen without clipping. Compare didn't disappear: it's a section of Insights now, alongside the AI insights and situation analytics, and every old Compare link or saved comparison lands there intact. One quiet improvement for families: a child's profile now sees the Insights tab too — with the comparison tools that were always age-neutral — while the training-restricted content stays hidden.

operatorNotes: For self-hosters who run the test suite: local e2e now uses per-worker databases and requires a production build first (the harness builds automatically when stale); parallel workers are supported and honest. No change to running or deploying the app itself.

entries.title: One Body tab, one place to log your numbers
entries.body: Trends loses its Vitals/Body split: one Body tab now leads with today's readings and the 1D intraday view, then your vitals charts (blood pressure, oxygen, resting heart rate — charted exactly once, goal line intact — HRV, and the fever view), then weight and body fat, with the tab strip down to six entries and old Vitals links landing in the right place. Logging is one combined "Log measurements" form — weight, body fat, blood pressure, glucose, oxygen, temperature, sleep, HRV, and growth fields for kids — behind a + Log button on desktop and the quick-log sheet's single Measurements item on your phone. The three fitness-check tests (grip, chair stand, balance) moved to the guided flow on Training, where timed tests belong — same records, same percentiles.

entries.title: Settings, reorganized around what things are about
entries.body: Settings is no longer three navigation systems around two very long pages: it's now an index of eleven topic groups — Account & security, Display & units, Health profile, Training, Nutrition, Coaching & AI, Notifications, Privacy, plus the admin People & access, Server, and Logs & audit — each a short page that states who it applies to (your login, this profile, or the server). The Notifications page drops from three screens to three sections with exactly one row per message kind (enable, timing, and channels together — the old duplicate toggle-card and routing matrix are gone, with no change to what's configurable). The active-sessions list finally reads as devices ("Chrome · Linux") instead of 22 identical truncated browser strings, collapsed to the recent few. One heads-up: old settings URLs from before the reorganization aren't redirected — use the index once and you're re-oriented.

entries.title: Your Trends Overview is now yours to curate
entries.body: The Overview tab shows exactly two things: what changed (the movers digest) and what you starred — nothing unconditional. The standard tiles (weight, body fat, resting heart rate, training volume) are still there on day one, but as ordinary saved tiles you can unstar or reorder like anything else; the domain tabs keep showing everything. Tiles also got denser on phones — two abreast, the latest value as the headline number, controls tucked into a corner menu — and a saved metric with no readings in the window compacts to a one-line row below the populated tiles instead of a full-height empty box. Unstar everything and the page tells you how to build it back rather than going blank.

entries.title: Dates read one way everywhere
entries.body: A sweep over every visible date: the same style now means the same thing across pages (day-of-week where it helps, the year only when it isn't this year), timestamps stop mixing formats mid-page, and a handful of form papercuts went with it — labels no longer clip their descenders, and disabled fields actually look disabled instead of just refusing input.

entries.title: Trends opens on the last 90 days
entries.body: Trends now defaults to a 90-day window instead of all time, so every chart leads with recent change rather than a lifetime average — and "All time" is still one tap away (links and saved views that meant all-time keep meaning it). A saved biomarker with no readings in the window shows its latest reading with an honest age ("55 ng/mL · 5 mo ago") instead of an empty tile, so stale never reads as current.

entries.title: Upcoming rows get one menu, and copy reads right
entries.body: Preventive items on Upcoming showed two identical "⋯" menus (two independent menus composing on one row) — now one merged menu, with a fixed-width status column so the Overdue label stops jumping and a mobile action row that folds secondary actions into the menu instead of wrapping. A copy sweep also fixed a subtle rendering bug that ate the space after bold text on ten pages, singular/plural slips ("1 errors"), and developer jargon in help text.

entries.title: Health-record pages read as one family
entries.body: The Problems tab joins the records pattern — Conditions and Allergies as proper sub-pages with the family's pill navigation, so an allergy link lands on the list itself. Filters unify into one outline-pill style across the record tabs, heading sizes settle into one hierarchy, and the journal's form-check section now appears only on activities that actually have clips, with adding one moved into the activity editor.

entries.title: Share a lab PDF straight into your record
entries.body: Install the app and your phone's share sheet gains an Allos target: share a PDF or a photo of a document from any app and it lands in the medical-upload pipeline — same per-person storage, duplicate detection, and AI extraction as the upload form — then opens the stored document so you can watch extraction and reassign it if it belongs to another family member. The upload form also gains a take-a-photo option on phones.

entries.title: Home-screen shortcuts and a badge that counts what needs you
entries.body: Long-press the installed app's icon for shortcuts straight into logging — food, a dose, weight, vitals, an activity, or search. The app icon also carries a badge with the same count as the dashboard's Needs-attention card, clearing when the day is handled (refreshes on open in this first version).

entries.title: Overlays that move as one, and swipes that go somewhere
entries.body: The drawer, bottom sheets, and the workout dock now share one motion system — same timing, same drag handle, same scrim — and one drag gesture with the right outcome per surface: swiping a sheet down dismisses it, swiping the workout dock minimizes it (a live workout is never discardable by gesture). The drawer opens with an edge swipe, and the Timeline's day view pages between days with a horizontal swipe or its new arrows. All of it is instant under reduced-motion.

entries.title: Redose guidance with just an interval, and a household dose round
entries.body: Setting only a minimum interval on an as-needed medication now shows the "Next dose in ~Nh" guidance — it previously required the optional daily maximum too. And caregivers can subscribe their Telegram reminder to a household round: one message covering the family members you select, each section with one-tap confirms that check your current access at the moment you tap and answer honestly if a dose was already handled.

entries.title: One star to save it everywhere
entries.body: Starring and pinning were two separate gestures for the same intent — a biomarker you cared about had to be starred for the Results status card and separately pinned to earn a Trends chart tile, and the two sets silently drifted apart. They're now one: starring a biomarker puts it on the Results card, gives it a Trends chart tile, and includes it in the profile summary, with a reorder control on Trends replacing the old pin toggle. Existing stars and pins merge automatically, keeping each save's original date and your tile order. One change to know: restoring a saved Trends view no longer alters which biomarkers are saved — views keep their date range and compare state only.

entries.title: Tables become cards on your phone
entries.body: Wide tables no longer ask for a sideways swipe on a phone: below tablet width the biomarkers table and the training Analyze table re-stack as readable cards — same data, labeled fields, nothing hidden. The biomarker panel, category, and notes columns that used to be dropped on small screens come back as labeled lines, and sorting stays available through a compact selector. More tables convert as they're next touched.

entries.title: Quick-log never takes you away
entries.body: Every item on the mobile quick-log sheet — food, dose, weight, and now vitals — opens its form right where you are and returns you there after saving, instead of navigating you to another page mid-check. The dose option shows today's due doses with one-tap confirms that answer honestly (a dose someone else already marked, or a paused medication, says so instead of claiming "logged"). Confirmation dialogs now rise as thumb-reachable sheets on phones, and the installed app gains pull-to-refresh.

entries.title: Vitals: today at a glance, and a real 1D view
entries.body: Trends → Vitals now leads with a Today strip — your latest readings with their times, linking to the day's timeline — and gains a 1D option that swaps the charts to a true intraday view: your minute-by-minute heart rate edge-to-edge on a phone (wear gaps shown as gaps, never bridged), with blood-pressure and oxygen readings placed at their actual clock times. The quick-add forms collapse to a "+ Log vitals" chip on mobile, taking the first chart from two screens down to inside the opening view.

entries.title: Charts you can actually tell apart
entries.body: The chart palette was rebuilt against real accessibility math — the two nearly-identical greens are gone (one is now a clear blue), warm colors darkened for contrast, and every future palette edit is auto-checked in CI for colorblind separation and contrast in both themes. Charts lose the gray default-grid look (quieter axes, dots only where they help, legends on every multi-series chart), heatmap calendars share one blessed color ramp, mini trend tiles become true sparklines with their range as text, and chart motion is a single quick draw-in that fully respects reduced-motion.

entries.title: The dashboard learns what time it is
entries.body: A compact "Now" strip tops the dashboard with the one or two of your existing cards that matter this minute — last night's sleep in the morning after your typical wake time, the workout recap in the hour after a session, nutrition around your mealtimes, the evening check-in while it's still unlogged. It promotes cards you already show (never one you've hidden), stays empty when nothing is timely, and your own grid order below is untouched. The "Needs attention" hero can now be collapsed to a one-line count on your phone — it always stays present with its count, and a day carrying a safety item (a missed critical dose) refuses to collapse at all.

entries.title: Trends opens on your charts
entries.body: On a phone, Trends used to spend almost two screens on date forms and browsing aids before the first chart. Now the quick-range chips lead (with saved views riding the same row), the From/To form tucks behind a Custom… chip — already open when you arrive on a shared link with custom dates — the movers card shows its top three with the rest one tap away, and the starred-biomarker status card lives on Results → Biomarkers, its one home. First chart on the seeded profile: from about two screens down to inside the opening view. The Timeline gets the same tidier date controls for free.

entries.title: A phone-first shell
entries.body: On a phone the app now has its own chrome: the top bar slides away as you scroll and returns the moment you scroll up, taking the multi-profile "Viewing N profiles" banner with it so you always know whose data you're reading. The bar carries one-tap Search and a contextual + button that starts the current page's obvious log — food on Nutrition, a dose on Medications, weight on Body — with a quick-log sheet behind it for everything else. The drawer learns your most-visited pages as Frequent shortcuts (kept on your device only), spacing tightens below tablet width, and every animation honors your system's reduced-motion setting.

entries.title: Offline dose logs are timed right and never lie
entries.body: A dose you confirm without signal is now logged at the moment you tapped it — not when your phone reconnected — so adherence history reflects when you actually took it. Replays also go through the exact same checks as a normal tap: a medication you paused, a dose the day already resolved, or an entry that sat queued too long is parked in the review panel with a plain-language reason instead of being reported as synced. This also fixes a real bug where a queued confirm could log a dose — and burn supply — for a paused medication.

operatorNotes: Migration 113 applies automatically on first boot after pulling (folds starred biomarkers and trend pins into the new unified save store). No manual steps; downgrading past it afterward requires a backup restore, as with any migration.

Migration 114 applies automatically on first boot after pulling (seeds each profile's standard Overview tiles as saved rows so they become removable; existing profiles see an identical Overview on day one). No manual steps; downgrading past it afterward requires a backup restore, as with any migration.

entries.title: Share one bottle across the household
entries.body: A medication or supplement can now link to a shared bottle in the new household cabinet. Everyone's doses draw from the same count — each person at their own dose size — days-remaining reflects the whole household's pace, and a low bottle raises exactly one alert, never one per person. Items you don't share keep their private counts.

entries.title: Release notes, right here in the app
entries.body: This page is new. It ships with the app itself, so after an update you can see what changed without leaving Allos — even offline. The small dot on the What's new link marks notes you haven't read yet and clears when you visit.

entries.title: Steadier phone-at-the-gym flow
entries.body: During a live workout the screen now stays awake only while the workout is actually in front of you — minimizing it to the dock releases the screen again (previously the phone could stay awake indefinitely). The rest timer's finish and each set check-off also give a short vibration cue on phones that support it, skipped when reduced motion is on.

entries.title: A day at a glance on the Timeline
entries.body: Opening a single day on the Timeline now shows the day on a clock: your heart-rate curve, sleep and workout blocks, and small tick marks for the day's timed events. Tapping a tick jumps to that entry in the list below. The panel appears only when the day has that kind of data.

entries.title: Merge duplicate workouts in one step
entries.body: The same workout arriving from more than one source can now be merged as a whole group — the cluster card on Data → Review, or several entries selected together in the Journal. After a sync, near-certain duplicates are merged for you; every automatic merge is listed so you can look at what it did and undo it.

entries.title: Symptoms and photos gather onto the illness episode
entries.body: A symptom logged while an illness episode is open now attaches to that episode by itself, and a photo can be tagged to the specific symptom entry it shows. The episode page pulls it all together, so a sick week reads as one story instead of scattered entries.

entries.title: Faster family access editor
entries.body: The login-by-profile access grid now opens as one compact summary row per login, and the grant controls load only when you start editing that row. A household with many logins and profiles reaches the screen far quicker.

entries.title: Health Connect token stored hashed, plus per-sync record details
entries.body: The token your phone uses to push Health Connect data is now stored hashed. It is shown once when you create it and can be replaced at any time with Rotate. Each recorded sync can also be opened to see exactly which records it added and which it updated.

entries.title: Sun and outdoor time on Trends
entries.body: Trends → Vitals now charts daylight and outdoor time alongside your other vitals. A per-profile setting for which days are free of a fixed schedule sharpens the social jetlag reading for anyone whose week is not Monday to Friday.

entries.title: Allergies and gene results name the medications they affect
entries.body: An allergy row now lists the active medications it conflicts with, and a pharmacogenomic variant row lists the medications it affects — the same warnings, and the same dismissals, already shown on the medication side. Procedures and conditions also link back to the visit they came from.

entries.title: Report narratives now visible
entries.body: Narrative text read out of a report — ECG, stress test, imaging — is now shown on Results → Reports instead of being stored where nothing displayed it.

entries.title: Biomarkers for several people at once
entries.body: Results → Biomarkers can now show more than one household member together, each with their own section, reference ranges and starred markers.

operatorNotes: Health Connect ingest tokens can no longer be re-displayed after this upgrade. Use Rotate on the Health Connect page to mint a new one; phones already paired keep working with their existing token.
Database migrations 109–111 apply automatically on the first boot after upgrading.
